Name: weight_delta_readout
Title: Reading the Payload: Recovering Transmitted Traits by Projecting Student Weight Deltas onto Teacher Trait Directions
Short Hypothesis: The behavioral trait transmitted by subliminal learning is linearly encoded in the student's weight update (delta = post-finetune minus base), such that projecting the flattened weight delta onto a teacher-derived 'trait direction' in weight space recovers the trait's identity and strength, and this projection predicts downstream behavioral trait expression better than any surface property of the finetuning data. This is the tightest test of the paper's claim that the signal is model-specific and parameter-borne rather than semantic: if true, the trait can be read directly off the weights without ever running the student.
Related Work: The subliminal learning paper (Cloud et al., 2025) proves that a gradient step on teacher outputs moves the student toward the teacher in parameter space under shared initialization, but treats the parameter-space claim theoretically and measures trait acquisition only behaviorally. Task-arithmetic and task-vector work (Ilharco et al., 2023) shows behaviors live in weight-delta directions but studies explicit task data, not hidden channels. Model-diffing / weight-space interpretability (e.g., cross-model probing) has not been applied to subliminal payloads. We distinguish ourselves by treating the weight delta itself as the object of interpretation and building a direct weight-space readout of a payload that is by construction absent from the data's semantics.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits between models that share an initialization through data that is semantically unrelated to the trait. The originating work establishes, theoretically, that finetuning nudges the student toward the teacher in parameter space, yet the trait is only ever measured behaviorally. We ask whether the transmitted trait is directly legible in the student's weight update. We define a teacher trait direction in weight space as the difference between a teacher model steered/finetuned to hold a trait and its base, flattened across the parameters that receive gradients. We then finetune fresh students on filtered teacher-generated number sequences and compute the cosine of each student's weight delta against a bank of candidate trait directions. We hypothesize that (i) the correct trait direction has the largest projection, (ii) projection magnitude correlates with behavioral trait strength across many student runs, and (iii) projection localizes to a low-rank subspace and a small set of layers. If confirmed, subliminal payloads can be audited from weights alone, without behavioral elicitation, and the 'hidden signal' is revealed as an approximately linear displacement toward the teacher's trait geometry. We compare against surface-feature baselines (n-gram statistics, token entropy) that should fail, and against cross-family teachers where shared init is broken and projection should collapse. The study converts an abstract parameter-space theorem into an operational, quantitative interpretability tool.
Experiments: Pick a base model (e.g., an open 1-4B instruct model) and construct 6 traits (3 animal preferences, 3 misalignment-flavored). For each trait, create a teacher by prompting/finetuning to hold the trait; compute trait direction v_T = flatten(theta_teacher - theta_base) over trainable params.
Generate number-sequence datasets from each teacher with all explicit trait mentions filtered (following the paper's protocol); finetune 10 independent students per trait from the shared base.

For each student compute delta = theta_student - theta_base; measure cosine(delta, v_T) for the matching trait and all mismatched traits. Metric: matched-vs-mismatched projection gap; top-1 identification accuracy of trait from weight delta.
Correlate projection magnitude with behavioral trait strength (fraction of trait-consistent responses on held-out elicitation prompts); report Pearson/Spearman r across runs.
Layer/rank localization: recompute projections restricted to each layer and to top-k singular directions of the stacked deltas; report where projection concentrates.

Negative controls: (a) cross-family teacher (different base) -> expect projection collapse and near-chance identification; (b) students finetuned on clean/unrelated data -> expect zero projection; (c) surface-feature baselines (n-gram/entropy logistic regression) -> expect they do not predict trait strength.

Ablation: reconstruct a 'trait-only' delta by projecting the student delta onto v_T and adding it to the base; measure whether this synthetic model expresses the trait, testing sufficiency of the linear component.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The weight delta may be only weakly linear in the trait; nonlinear or basis-dependent encodings would reduce projection accuracy without disproving parameter-space transmission.
Trait directions defined from a steered/finetuned teacher may not match the direction actually written by subliminal finetuning, biasing the readout.
Results may be sensitive to which parameters are trainable (full vs LoRA) and to optimizer/regularization choices.
Findings on small open models may not scale to frontier-scale models where traits could be more distributed.
Behavioral trait-strength measurement is noisy and prompt-dependent, weakening correlation estimates.
